title: Capsular Phimosis: Pathophysiology, Management & Prevention
summary: Capsular Phimosis (Capsulorhexis Contraction Syndrome) is the centripetal constriction of the anterior capsulorhexis opening following cataract surgery. This comprehensive guide covers the molecular mechanisms, high-risk populations, and advanced management strategies for ophthalmology residents and fellows.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Capsular phimosis is the fibrotic contraction of the anterior capsulorhexis opening (ACO) following Phacoemulsification. It results from the metaplasia and proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells (LECs) into myofibroblasts, which exert centripetal contractile forces on the capsular bag. While mild contraction is common, severe phimosis can lead to IOL decentration, zonular dialysis, and significant visual impairment.

sections.title: Etiology & Risk Factors
content: Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PEX): Weak zonules fail to counteract contractile forces.
Small Capsulorhexis: Openings <5.0mm are significantly more prone to phimosis.
IOL Material: Silicone lenses (especially 3-piece) show higher rates than hydrophobic acrylic.
Chronic Inflammation: Uveitis increases cytokine release (TGF-beta).
Myotonic Dystrophy & Retinitis Pigmentosa: Associated with early and severe contraction.
Inadequate Cortical Cleanup: Residual LECs are the primary engine of fibrosis.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: Step 1: Surgical trauma triggers cytokine release (TGF-β, IL-1, IL-6) into the aqueous humor.
Step 2: Residual A-cells (Lens Epithelial Cells) migrate from the equatorial region to the anterior capsule margin.
Step 3: Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) converts LECs into myofibroblasts.
Step 4: Expression of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) within myofibroblasts.
Step 5: Coordinated centripetal contraction of the fibrotic membrane, reducing the ACO diameter.

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Progressive IOL Decentration: Indicates asymmetric zonular failure.
Sunset Syndrome: Inferior subluxation of the IOL/capsular bag complex.
Anterior Displacement of IOL: Causes a 'myopic shift' and shallowing of the anterior chamber.
Vitreous in the Anterior Chamber: Sign of frank zonular dialysis.
Peripheral Retinal Tears: Resulting from excessive centripetal traction on the vitreous base.

sections.title: Neodymium:YAG Laser Management
content: 1. Dilate the pupil fully to visualize the fibrotic edge.
2. Apply topical anesthesia (e.g., Proparacaine).
3. Use a YAG-laser offset of 0 to +100μm.
4. Energy: 1.2 – 2.5 mJ per pulse.
5. Create 4 to 6 radial relaxing incisions (Cruciate pattern).
6. Post-op: Topical NSAIDs or Steroids for 3-5 days; monitor IOP.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention (Advanced Cases)
content: Manual Capsulectomy: Use micro-scissors (Vannas) to excise the fibrotic ring.
Plasma Blade (Fugo Blade): High-frequency cutting to reopen the ACO.
IOL Exchange: Required if the IOL is severely damaged or permanently decentered.
Scleral Fixation: If zonular loss is >4 clock hours, the bag-IOL complex may require sutured fixation (Gore-Tex or Yamane).

sections.title: Intraoperative Prevention Strategies
content: Optimal Rhexis Size: Aim for 5.5mm to 6.0mm (never <5.0mm).
Capsular Polishing: Thoroughly polish the underside of the anterior capsule to remove A-cells.
IOL Selection: Choose hydrophobic acrylic with sharp square edges.
Capsular Tension Ring (CTR): Distributes contractile forces; essential in PEX patients.
Large Optic IOLs: 6.0mm optics provide more mechanical resistance to contraction than 5.0mm optics.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Early intervention is easier: YAG is much more effective before the fibrosis becomes 'woody'.
Zonular check: If you see the IOL 'shaking' during YAG, the zonules are already compromised.
The 'Aqueous Outflow' theory: Chronic inflammation leads to higher levels of TGF-beta in the aqueous, fueling the myofibroblasts.
In RP patients, perform prophylactic YAG relaxing incisions 1-month post-op if contraction is seen.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: With timely YAG laser anterior capsulotomy, the visual prognosis is excellent. The ACO usually remains stable after radial incisions are made. However, if zonular dialysis has already occurred, the patient may face long-term risks of IOL subluxation requiring complex vitreoretinal intervention.
